item.text:
Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.

Rainfall varies because the atmosphere is always moving and changing. The amount of water vapor, the temperature of the air, the strength of upward motion, and the time a cloud remains over one area all affect how much rain falls. Gentle, widespread lifting can produce steady rain over a large region. Strong upward currents can build tall storm clouds and bring brief, heavy downpours. Mountains can force moist air upward and cause rain on one side, while the air descending on the other side becomes warmer and drier.

After rain reaches the ground, some water runs into streams and rivers, some soaks into the soil, and some gathers in lakes or the ocean. Some evaporates again, and plants return some to the air through transpiration. This repeating movement of water between the surface and atmosphere is part of the water cycle. Rain is one stage of that cycle: water rises as vapor, cools and condenses in clouds, and eventually returns to Earth as falling droplets.

Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface.

Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.

For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

Gentle, widespread lifting can produce steady rain over a large region. Strong upward currents can build tall storm clouds and bring brief, heavy downpours. Mountains can force moist air upward and cause rain on one side, while the air descending on the other side becomes warmer and drier.

After rain reaches the ground, some water runs into streams and rivers, some soaks into the soil, and some gathers in lakes or the ocean. Some evaporates again, and plants return some to the air through transpiration. This repeating movement of water between the surface and atmosphere is part of the water cycle. Rain is one stage of that cycle: water rises as vapor, cools and condenses in clouds, and eventually returns

Rain forms when water vapor in the air cools and becomes liquid droplets. The process begins at Earth’s surface, where sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants. Some liquid water evaporates: its molecules gain enough energy to leave the surface and enter the air as invisible water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, a process called transpiration. Together, evaporation and transpiration move water from the surface into the atmosphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. As the sun heats the ground, the air above it often warms too. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Air can also be pushed upward when winds meet, when it travels over hills and mountains, or when weather systems cause broad areas of air to lift. Rising air expands because the air pressure around it decreases with height. Expansion uses energy, so the air cools.

As the air cools, it eventually reaches a temperature at which it cannot keep all its water vapor in the gas form. This temperature is called the dew point. When air reaches the dew point, water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. Condensation happens more easily when tiny particles, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen, are present. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. They are called condensation nuclei.

The droplets that form are extremely small. A cloud is made of many such droplets, or, in cold conditions, of tiny ice crystals. Clouds form when enough droplets or crystals gather in a region of air to become visible. The droplets do not appear all at once in a single instant; they form and change continually as water vapor condenses and droplets mix with the surrounding air.

A cloud does not automatically produce rain. Its droplets are usually so small that air currents can keep them aloft. For rain to fall, droplets must grow large enough that gravity pulls them downward faster than rising air can carry them up. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly by colliding and joining together. Larger droplets fall through the cloud, bump into smaller ones, and collect them. This process is called collision and coalescence. As the droplets merge, they become heavier and fall more quickly, creating more opportunities to gather additional water.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor can deposit directly onto ice crystals, while some liquid droplets remain unfrozen even below the usual freezing point. The ice crystals grow as they collect water vapor and collide with other particles. They may become snowflakes, or they may grow by collecting supercooled droplets. If they become heavy enough, they fall. As they pass through warmer air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they remain frozen, they may fall as snow or another form of frozen precipitation.

A falling raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension pulls their water into a compact shape. Larger drops flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them while they fall. If they become too large, they can break apart into smaller drops. This limits how big ordinary raindrops tend to grow.

Whether precipitation reaches the ground depends on the air beneath the cloud. A raindrop may evaporate before it arrives if it falls through a layer of dry air. This creates a streak beneath the cloud called virga. If the lower air is moist enough, the drops survive their descent and reach the surface. Wind can move rain sideways, so it may fall far from the place where the cloud first formed.
